title: The Hard Questions at the Table
subtitle: Six sessions for the table where doubt sits, with every objection stated at full strength before anyone answers it
summary: Most churches handle the hard questions by not handling them, and the people carrying those questions eventually carry them out the door. This table works differently. Six sessions take the six questions that end more faith than any others, suffering, the violence in the Bible, the hypocrisy of the church, science, hell, and the question hiding under all of them, and state each objection at its full strength first, in the form its best defenders would recognize, before anyone at the table responds. The rule of the table is honesty, not victory. Nobody is scored, nobody is cornered, and I do not know is an honored answer. The doubter at this table is not a project. They are often the most honest person in the room.
setting: A living room or a quiet booth, small enough that nobody performs. Believers and doubters together, with the doubters knowing in advance that the objections will be stated fairly.
forWho: The Christian whose questions have nowhere safe to go, the skeptic willing to think out loud with honest company, and the friend who loves someone in either seat.
rhythm: Six sessions, an hour or a little more. Do not rush these. One session every two weeks is fine if the conversations run long, and they will.
leaderNote: Read the rule out loud at the first session and keep it all six: the objection gets stated at full strength before any response, and the table's job is honesty, not victory. If the skeptic at your table could not have put the objection better themselves, you have not stated it yet. Never let the room rescue God with a quick answer, and never shame a question. You will be asked things you cannot answer. Say so, write the question down where everyone can see you do it, and bring back what you find. The doubters at your table have usually been handled before. Do not handle them. Sit with them.

sessions.title: If God Is Good, Why This
sessions.bigIdea: The problem of suffering is the oldest and strongest objection to God, and the Bible does not answer it the way a philosophy seminar would. It gives a psalm that ends in the dark, and a God who stands at a grave and weeps.
sessions.open: Without fixing it or explaining it, name a suffering, yours or someone's you love, that made the question of God unavoidable. The table will just listen.
sessions.read: State the objection at full strength first. David Hume, in his Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion, published in 1779, sharpened a question as old as Epicurus: if God is willing to prevent evil but not able, he is weak. If he is able but not willing, he is not good. If he is both, why is there evil? Every person at this table has felt some version of that, and no answer should be attempted until its weight is felt. Now read Psalm 88:13-18, the one psalm that never turns upward, ending with the words, my companions have become darkness. The believers who assembled the Bible left it in. Then read John 11:32-35. Mary tells Jesus that if he had been there her brother would not have died, and Jesus, standing before the tomb he is about to open, wept.
observe: Psalm 88 is a prayer of faith that ends without relief. What does its presence in Scripture say about what God is willing to have said to him?
Jesus knows Lazarus will be alive within minutes. Why do you think he weeps anyway?
talk: Whether you believe or not: which response to suffering have you actually received from religious people, the quick explanation or the shared silence? What did each one do to you?

Hume's trilemma assumes we could see all the reasons a good God might have or not have. Is that assumption obviously true? And notice the other edge: if there is no God, is suffering even wrong, or just what matter does? Push on both sides honestly.

Christianity's strangest claim here is not an explanation but an event, that God entered the suffering himself, wept at a grave, and died screaming a psalm of abandonment. Does a God with scars change the question for you at all, even if it does not answer it?
sessions.practice: Sit with one suffering person this week, in person, and do not explain anything. Presence only. If your own suffering is the live one, read Psalm 88 once and notice that the Bible gave you these words to pray.
sessions.send: The table did not solve the problem of pain tonight. It refused to lie about it. That is the beginning of any answer worth having.
sessions.passItOn: Someone you know left faith, or refuses it, over a suffering nobody would sit with. Tell them what this table did tonight, stated the objection at full strength and did not flinch, and ask if they would come state theirs.

sessions.title: The Violence in the Book
sessions.bigIdea: The hardest texts in the Bible are actually in the Bible, and pretending otherwise fools no one. Honesty reads the conquest of Jericho out loud, then notices that the sharpest moral protest against God, shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just, is also in the Bible, on the lips of a believer.
sessions.open: What is a passage or story in the Bible that has genuinely bothered you, or that a friend has thrown at you and you had no answer for? Name it without softening it.
sessions.read: The objection first, at full strength. Richard Dawkins, in The God Delusion, published in 2006, called the God of the Old Testament arguably the most unpleasant character in all fiction, and backed the charge with a list: the flood, the plagues, and above all the conquest commands. He is pointing at real texts. So read one of them without flinching, Joshua 6:20-21, where the wall falls and they devoted all in the city to destruction, both men and women, young and old, oxen, sheep, and donkeys, with the edge of the sword. Sit in the discomfort before moving. Then read Genesis 18:25, where Abraham, arguing with God over Sodom, says, far be it from you to do such a thing, to put the righteous to death with the wicked. Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?
observe: Read Joshua 6:21 again slowly. What does the text actually say happened? Resist the urge to soften it or rush past it.
In Genesis 18, who is morally cross examining whom? What does God do with Abraham's protest, silence it or engage it?
talk: Start where the skeptic is strongest: if you heard of any army today claiming God told them to do what Joshua 6 describes, you would call it an atrocity. What makes that instinct right, and where did the standard we are judging by come from?

The texts themselves put weight on the other side of the scale: Genesis says the judgment waited four hundred years for the wickedness of the land to be complete, Rahab and her family were spared for faith, and the same standard later falls on Israel itself, exiled by the same justice. Does judgment aimed at wickedness rather than ethnicity change the charge, partly, fully, or not at all? Disagree freely.

Abraham's protest is Scripture. The Bible contains the complaint against the Bible. What does it mean that the tradition preserved the argument instead of sanding it off, and what does it permit you to say to God?
sessions.practice: Read the story of Rahab this week, Joshua 2 and Joshua 6:22-25, the Canaanite woman inside the judgment story who is spared and ends up in the family line of Jesus in Matthew 1. Write down what her presence does, and does not do, to your reading of the conquest.
sessions.send: The wound in the question was honored tonight, and the texts were read whole. Keep arguing like Abraham, face to face, rather than walking away behind God's back.
sessions.passItOn: Next time a friend quotes the worst verse they know, do not duck. Read it with them, whole, and then read Genesis 18:25 beside it. An unafraid reader is rarer than an answer, and more persuasive.

sessions.title: The Hypocrites
sessions.bigIdea: The critique of religious hypocrisy is not an attack on Jesus. It is a quotation of him. Nobody in history said it harder than the man who called the clergy whitewashed tombs, and no honest table defends what he condemned.
sessions.open: Tell the table, gently but truly, about a time religious people made faith harder for you to believe, not easier. What did it break?
sessions.read: The objection at full strength: the church preaches love and shelters abusers, preaches generosity and builds empires, preaches truth and covers up. These are not inventions of hostile critics. Some of the worst of it has been documented by courts and by the churches' own commissioned reports, and every person at this table can name a scandal without help. Now read Matthew 23:27-28, where Jesus says of the religious leaders, woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites. For you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but within are full of dead people's bones and all uncleanness. Then read Romans 2:24, where Paul tells religious people, the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you.
observe: Who receives the harshest words anywhere in Jesus' recorded teaching, the irreligious or the religious? What exactly is his charge against them?
Paul says the watching world's contempt is because of you, the religious insiders. Does the Bible treat hypocrisy as a rare exception or a standing danger?
talk: The hypocrisy objection assumes a standard: that the church should live what it preaches. Where does that standard come from, and what is strange about using Jesus' own measuring stick to dismiss Jesus?

For the believers at the table, the harder half: hypocrisy is not only a scandal in the headlines. It is a temptation at this table, being kinder in public than at home, louder about others' sins than our own. Where does the whitewash run in your own life? Go first, leaders.

A movement is fairly judged by its founder and by what its texts demand, and also by its honest practitioners, the quiet ones who never trend. Who is the least hypocritical Christian you have personally known, and what do you do with their evidence?
sessions.practice: Close one gap this week between your public self and your private one. Small and concrete: an apology owed at home, a criticism you make of others that you will say about yourself first. Hypocrisy shrinks one confession at a time.
sessions.send: Jesus is not the defense attorney for the church's hypocrisy. He is its oldest and angriest prosecutor. You can stand with him against it without leaving him.
sessions.passItOn: When a friend says the church is full of hypocrites, try the honest reply: you are right, it is, and Jesus said it first, and I am one of the milder cases. Then invite them to a table where that gets admitted out loud.

sessions.title: Science and the Faith
sessions.bigIdea: The story that science and Christianity have always been at war has a birthplace, two books from 1874 and 1896, and historians of science have largely taken it apart. The psalmist thought the heavens were evidence, and a priest proposed the expanding universe.
sessions.open: Growing up, were you handed the idea that you would someday have to choose between science and God? Who handed it to you, a church, a classroom, the internet?
sessions.read: The objection at full strength: science explains by evidence what religion once explained by authority, its predictions work, its medicine heals, and it has corrected the church more than once, Galileo being the famous case. Why keep a hypothesis that keeps retreating? Now the history, honestly. The warfare framing was popularized by two books, John William Draper's History of the Conflict Between Religion and Science in 1874 and Andrew Dickson White's A History of the Warfare of Science with Theology in Christendom in 1896, and historians of science have spent decades dismantling it. A 2009 volume edited by the historian Ronald Numbers, Galileo Goes to Jail and Other Myths About Science and Religion, works through the legends one by one. The real record is tangled: the church funded astronomy for centuries, Galileo was indeed silenced and that wrong should be named plainly, and in 1927 the expanding universe behind what became big bang cosmology was proposed by Georges Lemaitre, a Belgian physicist who was also a Catholic priest. Then read Psalm 19:1-4, the heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky above proclaims his handiwork. And read Proverbs 25:2, it is the glory of God to conceal things, but the glory of kings is to search things out.
observe: Psalm 19 treats the sky as speech, pouring out knowledge without words. Is nature, in this psalm, a rival to God or a witness for him?
Proverbs calls the searching out of hidden things a glory. What posture toward investigation does that verse actually command?
talk: Be precise about what science can and cannot weigh in on. It answers how questions with superb authority. Can a measurement, even in principle, tell you whether your life means anything, whether cruelty is wrong, or why there is something rather than nothing? Where do those questions go if the lab cannot take them?

The believers owe the table an admission: churches have sometimes fought discoveries out of fear and read poetry as if it were a lab report, and the Galileo affair really happened. What does faith lose when it is afraid of a telescope, and what would unafraid faith look like?

If the universe is the work of a mind, science is reading the author's handwriting, which is roughly how many early scientists described their work. If it is not, science is still possible but its own foundations, why nature is ordered and why our minds can grasp it, go unexplained. Which picture do you find yourself living in, and why?
sessions.practice: Spend twenty minutes this week with something real, the night sky, a nature documentary, a long walk, and let yourself feel the scale of it. Write one sentence on what the wonder itself seemed to be saying, if anything.
sessions.send: You were handed a war that the historians could not find. Hand it back. The heavens have been declaring something all along. The argument is over what.
sessions.passItOn: Somebody you know is quietly holding faith and science apart like feuding relatives. Tell them about Draper, White, and the priest who proposed the expanding universe. The permission to stop choosing is a gift you can give in one conversation.

sessions.title: Hell
sessions.bigIdea: The objection deserves its full weight: eternal consequence for a finite life sounds monstrous. The complication is that the hard sayings about hell come mostly from Jesus himself, the man of the weeping and the cross, which forbids the easy move of keeping the gentle teacher and dropping the judgment.
sessions.open: What picture of hell were you handed, from church, cartoons, or fear, and who used it on you? Was it ever wielded as a weapon in your story?
sessions.read: Full strength first, no softening: how could a loving God allow, let alone appoint, unending punishment for beings he made, whose lives lasted seventy years? Would a good father torture even his worst child forever? If heaven requires forgetting the people who did not make it, is it still heaven? Those questions have driven more people from the faith than perhaps any other, and they deserve better than a shrug. Now the complication. Read Matthew 10:28, where Jesus says, do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell. The tenderest figure in Scripture speaks its severest warnings, and he speaks them in tears over Jerusalem rather than in triumph. Then read 2 Peter 3:9. The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.
observe: In Matthew 10:28, what does Jesus assume about which danger is greater, and to whom is he saying it, enemies or friends?
According to 2 Peter, what does God actually wish for people, and what is his delay evidence of?
talk: Half the objection assumes hell is God gleefully torturing the unwilling. C.S. Lewis, in The Problem of Pain, published in 1940, argued the opposite picture: that the doors of hell are locked on the inside, judgment as God finally honoring a person's lifelong refusal of him. Does that reframe carry real weight for you, or does it feel like a philosopher's tidying of something Scripture leaves darker? Both answers are welcome at this table.

Now hold the other edge: a God who never judges is his own problem. Tell the victim of genocide, of abuse, of a trafficked childhood, that the ledger simply closes at death and nothing is ever set right. Is a universe without any final justice actually more loving, or only more comfortable for the unharmed?

Faithful Christians read the texts differently on the nature and duration of final judgment, and the church has argued the details for centuries. But notice where the weight of it drove people like Peter and Paul, not to gloating but to urgency and tears. Whatever hell is, what would taking it seriously do to how you treat the person across the street?
sessions.practice: Read Luke 15 this week, the lost sheep, the lost coin, the lost son, the same Jesus who spoke of hell describing the God who runs down the road to meet a returning child. Hold the two portraits together all week and write down what refuses to resolve.
sessions.send: The doctrine was not softened at this table tonight, and neither was the mercy. The one who warned of hell is the one who went to a cross to stand between you and everything he warned of.
sessions.passItOn: Someone you love was beaten with this doctrine, hell used as a whip rather than wept over. Go to them this week, name what was done to them as the distortion it was, and let them hear that the warning and the running Father come from the same mouth.

sessions.title: The Question Under the Questions
sessions.bigIdea: Many objections are load bearing walls built over a wound, a father, a funeral, a church that failed. The intellect deserves real answers, and got them at this table. But the last honest step is to ask what the questions are protecting, and the Bible has a prayer for exactly that split condition: I believe. Help my unbelief.
sessions.open: Five sessions in, answer as honestly as you can: which of the hard questions we have taken up is, for you, actually intellectual, and which one has a face or a date attached to it?
sessions.read: One more objection at full strength, aimed this time at the believers: religious people say doubt is really just woundedness so they can dismiss it without answering it. That move is real, it is condescending, and this table has refused it for five sessions, answering arguments as arguments. But the skeptics own version of honesty asks the mirror question: is every objection I hold purely intellectual, or are some of them guarding a door I do not want opened? Now read Mark 9:21-24. A father with a suffering son says to Jesus, if you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us. Jesus answers that all things are possible for one who believes, and the father cries out, I believe. Help my unbelief. Jesus heals the boy anyway. Then read John 6:66-69, where many disciples turn back and no longer walk with him, and Jesus asks the twelve if they want to leave too. Peter answers, Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life.
observe: The father in Mark 9 claims belief and unbelief in the same breath. How does Jesus respond to that divided man, rebuke or help?
Peter's answer in John 6 is not a proof. What kind of answer is it, and what has he weighed to give it?
talk: Trace one of your own hard questions back as far as it goes. Where did it start, a book, a betrayal, a hospital room, a house without a father? Naming the origin does not settle the argument, but what does it change?

Peter does not say every question is answered. He says, having looked at the alternatives, to whom shall we go? Do the honest work in both directions: what would it cost you to believe, and what would it cost you to keep not believing? Which cost have you been counting, and which have you been avoiding?

The prayer of Mark 9 is available tonight to anyone at this table, believer and doubter alike: I believe. Help my unbelief. What would you lose by praying it once this week, alone, as an experiment in honesty? If the answer is nothing, what is actually stopping you?
sessions.practice: Write two lists this week and show them to one person from this table: the questions you still hold, and what each question would require if it were answered. Then, if you are willing, pray the Mark 9 prayer once. Say it exactly as the father did, both halves.
sessions.send: You brought the questions and the table did not flinch. Whatever you decide, decide it awake, with the objections stated at full strength and the wound called by its name. He healed the boy of the half believing father. That is the kind of ground this table has been standing on all along.
sessions.passItOn: This table exists because someone believed doubters deserve honesty instead of handling. You have now sat through six sessions of it, whichever seat you sat in. Set the next table yourself, believer and doubter hosting together works best, and give the people you know the room nobody gave them.
